---
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/137360922/640511308/-1066768109?source=260816_km_measles&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNTkvMS8xMDkzOTAiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiYmI4OTVkOTgtY2U5OS1mMTExLTliMzMtMDAwZDNhMTFmYTMwIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=v5Jo6n5WIpTXtuyYnFcjIgxd7xHv19C4CJmk58DaM20=)
---
Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world.

It’s also one of the most preventable.

As a doctor, let me be clear up front: Measles can’t be cured or prevented with Vitamin A or cod liver oil. The _only_ reliable way to stop its spread is through vaccination.

So it’s both frustrating and frightening when avoidable public health outbreaks like this occur:
---
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/137360923/640511309/713978470?source=260816_km_measles&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNTkvMS8xMDkzOTAiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiYmI4OTVkOTgtY2U5OS1mMTExLTliMzMtMDAwZDNhMTFmYTMwIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=v5Jo6n5WIpTXtuyYnFcjIgxd7xHv19C4CJmk58DaM20=&emci=7c1faed1-2b97-f111-9b33-000d3a11fa30&emdi=bb895d98-ce99-f111-9b33-000d3a11fa30&ceid=26798886)
---
This isn’t random. It’s the direct result of stripping away public health programs and funding that used to keep outbreaks like this from happening in the first place — and the dangerous and widespread disinformation about vaccines this administration spreads.

**Bottom line: the record-high measles outbreak happening in our neighborhoods and families is the result of putting someone in charge of the country’s public health infrastructure who doesn't understand medicine, and who doesn’t trust science or experts. **

I care deeply about public health as a physician, as a mom, and as a human being. And I know exactly what vaccine misinformation costs — not in dollars, but in people's lives.

Before the measles vaccine, hundreds of children used to die every year from measles, thousands were hospitalized, and many suffered lifelong consequences. This new outbreak has already tragically cost two unvaccinated school-aged children their lives.

We don’t have to go back to a time when kids were dying from a disease that modern medicine solved decades ago. We just need leaders who trust doctors and believe in science over conspiracy theories.

**I will continue fighting the disinformation coming from Trump and RFK Jr, and I could really use you by my side — because the more voices we can add to the chorus, the more likely it is we will make a real impact.**

body:

Sorry to bug you so late tonight, but I couldn't go to sleep without
sending a quick email to say thank you.

The momentum over these past two weeks has been wild. Seeing three
separate polls show us within just 1 point of Greg Abbott has me totally

It's Scott Presler. I haven't reached out in a while, but I just got off the phone with my voter registration team in Pennsylvania, and I couldn't stay quiet. While we've been working day and night for the SAVE America Act, the Democrats quietly poured seven figures into voter registration — and it's working.
_Here's what they understand: the registration gains we made heading into 2024, funded $30 at a time by sponsors like you, were the difference maker. So now they've built a coordinated, well-funded response aimed squarely at erasing the advantage we spent years building._ I've never been an alarmist. But the latest numbers stopped me cold — and they're the reason I'm writing you today. There is no final victory in voter registration. We are always one month away from the Democrats surging ahead. _If we don't move now, we head into the midterms — and 2028 — at a serious disadvantage._ I need to hire and deploy more staff to Pennsylvania immediately. I can't do that without grassroots sponsors. Hey, folks --
Yesterday morning, the New York Times reported that Donald Trump's Department of Justice is investigating my company. Since then my phone hasn't stopped. **So let me start with the only thing that matters right now: thank you -- to every single one of you who reached out.**
Here's the whole sad arc, if you're just catching up. It started with Laura Loomer inventing a baseless conspiracy theory about my business. It moved to the House Judiciary Committee opening an investigation in 2024. And now it's Trump's DOJ. It is ridiculous that our government is being run by right-wing conspiracy theorists. But here we are.
We're going to be okay.

Friends, I want to talk to you about something that’s been keeping me up at night: the future of work in the age of AI.

The CEO of AI giant Anthropic has predicted _Great Depression levels of unemployment within the next five years_ , while Bill Gates has said that humans won't be needed at all for most things within a decade. Corporate leaders at Intuit, Oracle, and Block are already citing AI as the reason for mass layoffs. And young workers in AI-exposed careers are struggling to find jobs.

_The impacts of AI are already here, and the federal government has no real plan to deal with them._ Meanwhile, AI billionaires are positioning themselves to make _trillions_ off AI systems trained on human work and ultimately designed to push out workers.

**" Trump says Texas being against data centers is a mistake"** via [Dallas Morning News](https://substack.com/redirect/d0035fd4-3e3b-4fda-9c7a-40ea72f255eb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Lana Ferguson** - President **Donald Trump** has entered the Texas data center debate. In the same week that Gov. **Greg Abbott** called for state regulators to conduct a sweeping audit of data centers wanting to connect to Texas' power grid -- effectively putting those projects on hold -- Trump called Texas' opposition to data centers a mistake.

In a wide-ranging video interview published Friday, Trump discussed data centers and artificial intelligence on a national level but nodded to the drama playing out in communities across the Lone Star State. "What is going to be the political impact of data centers?" **Jake Sherman** asked. "I know you've taken action. Congress is going to try to take action. It's going to be in the next 10 years, a big political issue."

Trump began his answer focusing on artificial intelligence, saying "whoever wins AI just wins," then turned to Texas. "I saw Texas the other day is sort of against data centers," Trump said. "I think it's a mistake." Trump said he wasn't taking a position, clarifying: "I just think it's a mistake because there are communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community." _([DMN](https://substack.com/redirect/d0035fd4-3e3b-4fda-9c7a-40ea72f255eb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Hours before deadline, City Council will debate whether to call second Spurs arena vote"** via [San Antonio Report](https://substack.com/redirect/52057bad-07f3-4b2e-abc9-cf6f35a0b8f6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Andrea Drusch** and **Joey Palacios** - San Antonio City Council is headed for another heated debate over its plans for a new downtown Spurs arena.

On Monday, just hours before the state's deadline to add measures to the Nov. 3 ballot, the council will hold a special meeting to decide whether to seek voter support for a $489 million contribution to the overall $1.3 billion basketball arena.

The move isn't legally required, and most council members considered the spending a done deal after voters approved Bexar County's portion of the funding in Props A and B last November.

But **Gina Ortiz Jones** says the county vote was taken before taxpayers had a clear picture of the city's tough financial straits, and put her call for a separate city vote on Monday's agenda. _([SA REPORT](https://substack.com/redirect/52057bad-07f3-4b2e-abc9-cf6f35a0b8f6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Texas could owe $709M for food stamps. Food banks say the fallout would be 'catastrophic.'"** via [KSAT](https://substack.com/redirect/75c8ea15-e002-4ab0-9d4c-b8389d112581?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Hunter King** - Food banks across Texas are raising the alarm over a federal policy change that could force the state to pay hundreds of millions of dollars for food assistance benefits or risk leaving millions of Texans without access to food.

Beginning in 2027, states with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) payment error rates above 6% will be required to share in the cost of benefits under the "One Big Beautiful Bill," signed into law in 2025. Texas recorded a 9% error rate in fiscal year 2025, meaning the state could face up to $709 million a year in additional costs, and potentially more than $1 billion if that rate climbs above 10%.

San Antonio Food Bank CEO **Eric Cooper** said the stakes couldn't be higher. "When you think about the San Antonio Food Bank, for every one meal we put out, SNAP provides nine," Cooper said. "Should we see an increase in the number of families, we just won't have the food supply to meet that need."

**Celia Cole** , CEO of Feeding Texas, the state association of food banks, said the error rate triggering these new costs is widely misunderstood. "The most important thing to know about the payment error rate is that it is not fraud," Cole said. "It is a measure of accuracy." _([KSAT](https://substack.com/redirect/75c8ea15-e002-4ab0-9d4c-b8389d112581?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" How Texas is courting Wall Street with 'Y'all Street'"** via [The Washington Post](https://substack.com/redirect/a7ab97da-d4ef-4ba6-9a4d-3f30350f00b3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Andrew Ackerman** - Big banks are scaling up in Dallas while a new stock exchange opens for business in a state that has declared itself America's finance capital.

**Lenwood Brooks** spent years in Washington, most recently as chief of staff at an agency that oversees credit unions. When he left in 2023, he found what many of his industry peers were also discovering: All the jobs were in Texas.

The Mississippi native landed first at the Federal Home Loan Bank of Dallas, then jumped to the fast-growing Dallas outpost of an investment bank. Eager to lean into Texas culture, he took his real estate agent's advice and bought a $765 beaver-fur cowboy hat.

Brooks is a small part of a much larger shift. For years, financial firms and the people who staff them have been drifting toward the Lone Star State, drawn by low taxes, lighter-touch regulation and aggressive courting by political leaders. While the migration has been building for years, lately it has become impossible to miss -- especially in Dallas. Texas Gov. **Greg Abbott** already calls Texas the financial capital of America, and the numbers are hard to argue with: Finance jobs in Dallas have grown by 23.2 percent since February 2020 -- far faster than New York City's 6 percent increase -- even as such jobs remain below pre-pandemic levels in Chicago, Boston and San Francisco, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas. _([WAPO](https://substack.com/redirect/a7ab97da-d4ef-4ba6-9a4d-3f30350f00b3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" US Attorney confirms no meth was found in van of Texas man shot by immigration officers"** via [Houston Chronicle](https://substack.com/redirect/067a449b-dfc4-40d0-bea5-beca4ede71bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) - A federal prosecutor says tests on "a white crystal-like substance" found inside the van of a man shot to death by immigration officers in Houston last month showed the material was not methamphetamine.

U.S. Attorney **Aaron Reitz** confirmed the tests were negative for meth in a statement to The Texas Tribune, the news organization reported Thursday.

**Lorenzo Salgado Araujo** , 52, was killed July 7 when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in unmarked vehicles chased his white work van through the streets of Houston, then shot him through the window. He had been driving his work crew, including his brother, to a construction site. _([HOU CHRON](https://substack.com/redirect/067a449b-dfc4-40d0-bea5-beca4ede71bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Why Houston's bid for an NHL expansion team is different under Dan Friedkin"** via [Houston Chronicle](https://substack.com/redirect/49ebc426-e124-40da-8f56-6e0fbafb28c8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Greg Rajan** - Houston billionaire Dan Friedkin, no stranger to pro sports with his European soccer teams, is pursuing an NHL expansion franchise in Texas. Houston and Austin are being considered, with a decision to come in December.

The man who could bring Houston the city's long-awaited NHL franchise is staying mum for the moment. But as billionaire **Dan Friedkin** decides between Houston and Austin for the location of the NHL's 33rd franchise, it's becoming clear this effort is much further along than previous endeavors in the city's decades-long quest for a team in hockey's top league.

A spokesman for Pursuit Sports, Dan Friedkin's company dedicated to the family's sports properties, politely declined comment when asked how things are progressing nearly two months since NHL commissioner **Gary Bettman** announced the exploration of expansion in Texas. But deputy commissioner **Bill Daly** , the longtime right-hand man for Bettman, said Friedkin has brought a different dynamic than previous suitors.

Daly told the Houston Chronicle, "I think there's always a variety of kind of environmental factors that can play into any particular situation, either positive or negative," Daly said. "In Houston's case in particular, (it's) whether there's a suitable venue in which the hockey team can play. **" Trial lawyers, once a force for Democrats, reclaim political clout in Texas GOP's MAGA wing"** via [The Texas Tribune](https://substack.com/redirect/be5752f3-4d1b-4f28-a235-91653349599a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Eleanor Klibanoff** - When **Armin Mizani** won the GOP primary for a north Texas House district in March, warning bells went off in certain Republican circles. **" Senate candidates Ken Paxton and James Talarico propose different plans to help Texans with affordability"** via [CBS News](https://substack.com/redirect/fb1a2336-e2cb-430b-90d1-1c8076c58913?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Jack Fink** - With less than three months to go before the November election, Republican **Ken Paxton** and Democrat **James Talarico** introduced their economic agendas while campaigning in North Texas last week.

**" Are There Really Democrats for Paxton and Republicans for Talarico?"** via [Texas Monthly](https://substack.com/redirect/519976a4-f492-44f4-b763-d96df67217b7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Christopher Hooks** - Casting ballots across party lines used to be pretty common in Texas: It was a behavior folks had to unlearn. It wasn't until fairly recently in American life that there was a left-wing party and a right-wing party and voting patterns calcified. In 1952, Texas Republicans knew any gubernatorial candidate they put forward would lose to the conservative Democratic candidate and decided to give him their nomination too, so that the final result on Election Day was **Allan Shivers** versus Allan Shivers, 73 to 25. A decade later, in 1961, the first Republican to win statewide in Texas since Reconstruction, **John Tower** , won his Senate seat partly with the help of liberals, who hated his conservative Democratic opponent.

This produced a couple of decades in which Texas politics was unpredictable--in a way it wasn't before and hasn't been since. But the era of ticket switching came to an end around the turn of the century. In a time when people's ideological affinities tend to be perfectly matched with their partisan affinities, it's harder to pull them away from a straight-ticket ballot. For the past two decades, Democrats have hoped in each election that enough typically Republican-voting Texans would defect for one reason or another--business-minded moderates for **Bill White** in 2010, maybe, or pro-choice suburban women for **Wendy Davis** in 2014--and they haven't. If Democrats are to win a race this year, they're going to have to find a way.

Here's a strange thing, then, one of many that make this year unusual. Of the seven nonjudicial statewide races in Texas this year, three feature Republican candidates whose GOP-primary opponents have given Republican voters either tacit or explicit permission to vote Democratic. Republican agricultural commissioner **Sid Miller** , who lost his primary bid for renomination, appeared at an anti-data center rally with **Clayton Tucker** , the Democratic candidate, near Matagorda Bay last month. He has called Republican nominee **Nate Sheets** a "pathological liar and grifter." **Hawk Dunlap** , the fifth-place Republican candidate in the GOP primary for the oil-and-gas-regulating Railroad Commission of Texas, introduced the Democratic candidate at the state Democratic convention last month. _([TX MONTHLY](https://substack.com/redirect/519976a4-f492-44f4-b763-d96df67217b7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Plano calls November tax election to help fund proposed Dallas Stars arena"** via [Dallas Morning News](https://substack.com/redirect/f51f7dd3-0ec6-4faa-8ee4-629c33bf0976?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)' **Lilly Kersh** - The Plano City Council voted unanimously Monday night to call the November election, which will ask voters to consider several potential taxes meant to collect money from visitors and event attendees.

If approved, the taxes could make it more expensive to rent a car and stay in a hotel in Plano, or add fees to parking and to the cost of attending an event at the proposed arena. It could also allow the city to tax sports teams who play there.

The NHL franchise announced in June it had signed a nonbinding letter of intent to build an arena and entertainment district at ailing shopping mall's site in Plano. City officials then agreed to pitch in public funds for the project, including pursuing the fall election to add taxes.

Neighbors have spoken out against the project, concerned that the residential area around the mall is unfit for an arena and welcome fans on already crowded roads. **Judith Walsh** lives nearby and asked the council to pause the election efforts until the city can commit to "binding, enforceable neighborhood protection measures" like parking enforcement and traffic abatement. _([DMN](https://substack.com/redirect/f51f7dd3-0ec6-4faa-8ee4-629c33bf0976?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Austin targets 900+ people caught in a costly cycle of crisis care"** via [Austin American-Statesman](https://substack.com/redirect/61c64a87-4289-4303-adf0-a15f06e6b3b4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Austin Sanders** - Officials from more than a dozen local government agencies and nonprofit organizations are launching an effort to break a costly cycle of homelessness, psychiatric crises, emergency room visits and repeated arrests among some of Austin's most vulnerable residents.

The initiative, called No Wrong Door, brings together 17 city, county, health care and nonprofit organizations to identify people who repeatedly cycle through jails, hospitals and homelessness services and develop individualized plans to connect them with treatment and support.

Data included in a city report released Aug. 4 show a relatively small population accounts for an outsized share of arrests and other costly interactions with public systems. From 2021 through 2025, 2% of people arrested by Austin police accounted for 17% of all arrests. Among the frequent users of those systems, 85% had experienced homelessness and 55% had behavioral health issues, an umbrella term that includes severe mental illness and other issues like substance abuse disorder. _([AAS](https://substack.com/redirect/61c64a87-4289-4303-adf0-a15f06e6b3b4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**BUSINESS NEWS**
**" Mark Cuban withdraws petition against Mavericks, but dispute isn't over"** via [Dallas Morning News](https://substack.com/redirect/ffbb9813-7e5d-4e16-ad1a-58d3a85a71b5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)' **Brad Townsend** - Mavericks minority shareholder **Mark Cuban** has withdrawn his Rule 202 Petition against team governor **Patrick Dumont** and the case has been dismissed without prejudice -- but the dispute appears far from over.

Late Monday, Cuban's attorneys filed to Texas Business Court a notice of nonsuit without prejudice. Judge **Bill Whitehill** subsequently dismissed the case and cancelled the arbitration hearing scheduled for Friday.

Cuban's petition , originally filed in Dallas County's 134th District Court on July 8 and moved to Texas Business Court on July 31, accused Dumont of "adversarial business practices" and sought a pre-suit deposition to glean more details about the Mavericks' plans to build an arena and entertainment district.

Cuban's legal team, led by **John Zavitsanos** of Ahmad, Zavitsanos & Mensing PLLC, made it clear in Monday's filing that he intends to make sure he's kept in the loop on the Mavericks' arena plans, using legal means if necessary. _([DMN](https://substack.com/redirect/ffbb9813-7e5d-4e16-ad1a-58d3a85a71b5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" What to know about Elon Musk's potential $10B Tesla solar facility in Fort Bend"** via [Houston Chronicle](https://substack.com/redirect/9c3fb253-2751-4416-a968-917fb59a3114?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Erica Grieder** - Tesla is considering placing a $10 billion solar cell facility in Fort Bend County, according to state records, as **Elon Musk** continues to expand his operations in the Houston region.

The electric automaker on Aug. 6th filed for school district property tax abatements related to the project, which it says would be located in Lamar Consolidated Independent School District, a quickly growing district in the southwest of Houston.

The project represents a capital investment of $10.1 billion, Tesla said. Building the facility would also create 1,150 construction jobs over a three-year period, the filing said, with the plant launching operations in 2029. _([HOU CHRON](https://substack.com/redirect/9c3fb253-2751-4416-a968-917fb59a3114?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" What to know about SpaceX and Tesla's $17B chip plant near College Station"** via [Houston Chronicle](https://substack.com/redirect/fc44cccb-d877-4ba9-969c-68657626c5df?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Andrea Leinfelder** - SpaceX and Tesla are building a 100-million-square foot chipmaking facility outside of College Station in Grimes County, the companies confirmed on Thursday.

The $16.8 billion facility, dubbed Terafab, will make chips for the companies' self-driving vehicles, humanoid robots and space-based data centers. It's expected to employ more than 3,000 people.

Terafab is a planned semiconductor manufacturing facility. It's a joint project between SpaceX and Tesla, which are both based in Texas. **Elon Musk** , the CEO of both companies, unveiled Terafab in March, saying his future endeavors would require more chips than the global market could supply.

Elon Musk has previously said Terafab will create enough chips for a "terawatt of compute" each year. SpaceX is calling Terafab "epic in both its mission and in its sheer size." Musk shared renderings in a futuristic video posted to X on Thursday. Terafab is expected to have more than 100 million square feet of manufacturing space. For comparison, Giga Texas, where Tesla makes the Model Y electric SUV and Cybertruck, has more than 10 million square feet of factory floor, according to Tesla. _([HOU CHRON](https://substack.com/redirect/fc44cccb-d877-4ba9-969c-68657626c5df?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Old EDS 'God Pod' to be imploded for AT&T's new billion-dollar HQ"** via [Dallas Morning News](https://substack.com/redirect/a3d87f73-2e4d-4b2d-97eb-860e62d39c5f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)' **Nick Wooten** - Sunday marks the end of an era and the start of something new in Plano. Additional portions of the old Electronic Data Systems campus, including the futuristic executive office building dubbed the "God Pod," will be imploded Sunday morning. The demolition is no surprise. Telecommunications giant AT&T planned to demolish the entire slate of buildings and parking garages to build its new billion-dollar-plus global headquarters at 5400 Legacy Drive.

Plano officials told The Dallas Morning News "a planned controlled demolition" will take place on Parkwood Boulevard between Legacy Drive and Democracy Drive around 8 a.m. AT&T declined to comment on the demolition. KDC, the developer of AT&T's campus, said construction is underway and demolition has begun at the site's north end. The company declined to provide any additional details.

EDS' move to Plano in the late 1980s was the first in a flurry of moves that helped establish the Collin County suburb as a headquarters hotspot. EDS founder **Ross Perot** purchased 2,700 acres in west Plano to establish the master-planned Legacy business park. For his son, real estate developer **Ross Perot Jr.** , the site holds special memories. He learned to fly a helicopter there, and he remembers riding horses when the Plano parcels his father owned were just raw land. Perot Jr. said he toured the old EDS site a few months back with AT&T CEO **John Stankey** just before demolition began. Perot Jr. said he won't attend Sunday's implosion. _([DMN](https://substack.com/redirect/a3d87f73-2e4d-4b2d-97eb-860e62d39c5f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Pharmaceutical giant to bring $2.3B manufacturing plant, 500 jobs to Houston"** via [Houston Chronicle](https://substack.com/redirect/c6257fcd-4539-4f70-baf0-af57ab3fcda8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Erica Grieder** - Bristol Myers Squibb announced Monday that it will build a $2.3 billion advanced manufacturing facility in Houston's Generation Park, a coup for the region's growing biotech sector.

The new facility in northeast Houston will cover 600,000 square feet and create 500 jobs, according to the New Jersey-based pharmaceutical giant. Construction will begin next year and is expected to be completed by 2030, the company said, creating about 2,000 jobs during that three-year period.

The new facility "is designed to grow in scale, capability and workforce for decades to come," **Bristol Myers Squibb** said in a statement. "BMS envisions this site growing in scale and capability well beyond its opening configuration." _([HOU CHRON](https://substack.com/redirect/c6257fcd-4539-4f70-baf0-af57ab3fcda8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**TEXANS IN DC**
**" Cornyn Urges DHS to Hear Texas Concerns Before Big Bend Border Barrier Construction"** via [Texas Border Business](https://substack.com/redirect/446f3f7c-9b68-4bc3-bb76-6e392f3ea8ca?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) - Senator **John Cornyn** , R-Texas, has asked the Department of Homeland Security to meet with Texas stakeholders before proceeding with additional construction of physical border barriers in Big Bend National Park and Big Bend Ranch State Park.

Cornyn said Texas supports federal efforts to secure the U.S.-Mexico border while asking DHS to consider concerns specific to the Big Bend area.

"Texas has always worked cooperatively with the Department of Homeland Security ('DHS' or 'Department') on border security, and we fully support strong border security measures to stop the flow of illegal aliens, drugs, and potential terrorists into the United States," Cornyn wrote.

According to Cornyn, stakeholders contend that the geography surrounding Big Bend already presents significant obstacles to unauthorized crossings, and he described concerns from people who live and work near the parks about the potential environmental, cultural and economic effects of constructing a physical wall and related infrastructure, in a letter to DHS Secretary **Markwayne Mullin**. _([Texas Border Business](https://substack.com/redirect/446f3f7c-9b68-4bc3-bb76-6e392f3ea8ca?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Ted Cruz's college sports bill left in limbo as U.S. Senate takes August recess"** via Texas Tribune's **Samanta Habashy** - Sen. **Ted Cruz 's** bill that would place sweeping new regulations on college sports failed to reach the floor this week before the Senate gaveled out for recess, imperiling its chances to become law this year as the midterm elections approach.

The measure, coined the Protect College Sports Act, had gained a sudden burst of momentum with support from the Southeastern Conference and Big Ten, after spending weeks in limbo. It advanced out of the Senate Commerce Committee, which Cruz chairs, before the chamber was scheduled to adjourn Friday. President **Donald Trump** urged senators to stay until they got through a pile-up of his legislative priorities, including the college sports bill.

But the bill never came up on the floor before the chamber gaveled out at 3:56 a.m. Senators could still pass the bill after their scheduled return to Capitol Hill after Labor Day. Last week, Cruz and other lawmakers, along with White House officials, negotiated a package of concessions with Big Ten and SEC leaders, who until then had refused to back the bill.

"Without this Bill, millions of young Athletes will be hurt, programs will be canceled, Women's and Olympic Sports will go away, the fans will be robbed, and Universities will go broke," **Donald Trump** posted on social media Friday afternoon, urging the Senate to stop "grandstanding" and pass it before leaving town. Cruz's bill would place a host of new regulations on the free-for-all system that has emerged since the NCAA in 2021 allowed college athletes to profit off their name, image and likeness, followed by a settlement a few years later that required the NCAA and athletic conferences to share revenue with athletes. _([ABC13 Houston](https://substack.com/redirect/c4d71e99-6a8c-4837-b47e-d399d67904a8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

TOP NEWS " Trump says Texas being against data centers is a mistake" via Lana Ferguson - President Donald Trump has entered the Texas data center debate. In the same week that Gov. Greg Abbott called for state regulators to conduct a sweeping audit of data centers wanting to connect to Texas' power grid -- effectively putting those projects on hold -- Trump called Texas' opposition to data centers a mistake. In a wide-ranging video interview published Friday, Trump discussed data centers and artificial intelligence on a national level but nodded to the drama playing out in communities across the Lone Star State. "What is going to be the political impact of data centers?" Jake Sherman asked. "I know you've taken action. Congress is going to try to take action. It's going to be in the next 10 years, a big political issue." Trump began his answer focusing on artificial intelligence, saying "whoever wins AI just wins," then turned to Texas. "I saw Texas the other day is sort of against data centers," Trump said. "I think it's a mistake." Trump said he wasn't taking a position, clarifying: "I just think it's a mistake because there are communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community." () " Hours before deadline, City Council will debate whether to call second Spurs arena vote" via Andrea Drusch and Joey Palacios - San Antonio City Council is headed for another heated debate over its plans for a new downtown Spurs arena. On Monday, just hours before the state's deadline to add measures to the Nov. 3 ballot, the council will hold a special meeting to decide whether to seek voter support for a $489 million contribution to the overall $1.3 billion basketball arena. The move isn't legally required, and most council members considered the spending a done deal after voters approved Bexar County's portion of the funding in Props A and B last November. But Gina Ortiz Jones says the county vote was taken before taxpayers had a clear picture of the city's tough financial straits, and put her call for a separate city vote on Monday's agenda. () " Texas could owe $709M for food stamps. Food banks say the fallout would be 'catastrophic.'" via Hunter King - Food banks across Texas are raising the alarm over a federal policy change that could force the state to pay hundreds of millions of dollars for food assistance benefits or risk leaving millions of Texans without access to food. Beginning in 2027, states with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) payment error rates above 6% will be required to share in the cost of benefits under the "One Big Beautiful Bill," signed into law in 2025. Texas recorded a 9% error rate in fiscal year 2025, meaning the state could face up to $709 million a year in additional costs, and potentially more than $1 billion if that rate climbs above 10%. San Antonio Food Bank CEO Eric Cooper said the stakes couldn't be higher. "When you think about the San Antonio Food Bank, for every one meal we put out, SNAP provides nine," Cooper said. "Should we see an increase in the number of families, we just won't have the food supply to meet that need." **TOP NEWS**
**" Trump says Texas being against data centers is a mistake"** via [Dallas Morning News](https://substack.com/redirect/50a612cf-266c-4b0c-9350-d5bcfb26e313?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Lana Ferguson** - President **Donald Trump** has entered the Texas data center debate. In the same week that Gov. **Greg Abbott** called for state regulators to conduct a sweeping audit of data centers wanting to connect to Texas' power grid -- effectively putting those projects on hold -- Trump called Texas' opposition to data centers a mistake.

In a wide-ranging video interview published Friday, Trump discussed data centers and artificial intelligence on a national level but nodded to the drama playing out in communities across the Lone Star State. "What is going to be the political impact of data centers?" **Jake Sherman** asked. "I know you've taken action. Congress is going to try to take action. It's going to be in the next 10 years, a big political issue."

Trump began his answer focusing on artificial intelligence, saying "whoever wins AI just wins," then turned to Texas. "I saw Texas the other day is sort of against data centers," Trump said. "I think it's a mistake." Trump said he wasn't taking a position, clarifying: "I just think it's a mistake because there are communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community." _([DMN](https://substack.com/redirect/50a612cf-266c-4b0c-9350-d5bcfb26e313?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Hours before deadline, City Council will debate whether to call second Spurs arena vote"** via [San Antonio Report](https://substack.com/redirect/12646f42-c1ab-4dc1-809d-174bad6e7afd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Andrea Drusch** and **Joey Palacios** - San Antonio City Council is headed for another heated debate over its plans for a new downtown Spurs arena.

On Monday, just hours before the state's deadline to add measures to the Nov. 3 ballot, the council will hold a special meeting to decide whether to seek voter support for a $489 million contribution to the overall $1.3 billion basketball arena.

The move isn't legally required, and most council members considered the spending a done deal after voters approved Bexar County's portion of the funding in Props A and B last November.

But **Gina Ortiz Jones** says the county vote was taken before taxpayers had a clear picture of the city's tough financial straits, and put her call for a separate city vote on Monday's agenda. _([SA REPORT](https://substack.com/redirect/12646f42-c1ab-4dc1-809d-174bad6e7afd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Texas could owe $709M for food stamps. Food banks say the fallout would be 'catastrophic.'"** via [KSAT](https://substack.com/redirect/926b1c5a-76a3-4a83-9ad7-19e979209824?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Hunter King** - Food banks across Texas are raising the alarm over a federal policy change that could force the state to pay hundreds of millions of dollars for food assistance benefits or risk leaving millions of Texans without access to food.

Beginning in 2027, states with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) payment error rates above 6% will be required to share in the cost of benefits under the "One Big Beautiful Bill," signed into law in 2025. Texas recorded a 9% error rate in fiscal year 2025, meaning the state could face up to $709 million a year in additional costs, and potentially more than $1 billion if that rate climbs above 10%.

San Antonio Food Bank CEO **Eric Cooper** said the stakes couldn't be higher. "When you think about the San Antonio Food Bank, for every one meal we put out, SNAP provides nine," Cooper said. "Should we see an increase in the number of families, we just won't have the food supply to meet that need."

**Celia Cole** , CEO of Feeding Texas, the state association of food banks, said the error rate triggering these new costs is widely misunderstood. "The most important thing to know about the payment error rate is that it is not fraud," Cole said. "It is a measure of accuracy." _([KSAT](https://substack.com/redirect/926b1c5a-76a3-4a83-9ad7-19e979209824?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" How Texas is courting Wall Street with 'Y'all Street'"** via [The Washington Post](https://substack.com/redirect/5e4247e3-ff64-43c1-b389-02ec288a5c0e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Andrew Ackerman** - Big banks are scaling up in Dallas while a new stock exchange opens for business in a state that has declared itself America's finance capital.

**Lenwood Brooks** spent years in Washington, most recently as chief of staff at an agency that oversees credit unions. When he left in 2023, he found what many of his industry peers were also discovering: All the jobs were in Texas.

The Mississippi native landed first at the Federal Home Loan Bank of Dallas, then jumped to the fast-growing Dallas outpost of an investment bank. Eager to lean into Texas culture, he took his real estate agent's advice and bought a $765 beaver-fur cowboy hat.

Brooks is a small part of a much larger shift. For years, financial firms and the people who staff them have been drifting toward the Lone Star State, drawn by low taxes, lighter-touch regulation and aggressive courting by political leaders. While the migration has been building for years, lately it has become impossible to miss -- especially in Dallas. Texas Gov. **Greg Abbott** already calls Texas the financial capital of America, and the numbers are hard to argue with: Finance jobs in Dallas have grown by 23.2 percent since February 2020 -- far faster than New York City's 6 percent increase -- even as such jobs remain below pre-pandemic levels in Chicago, Boston and San Francisco, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas. _([WAPO](https://substack.com/redirect/5e4247e3-ff64-43c1-b389-02ec288a5c0e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" US Attorney confirms no meth was found in van of Texas man shot by immigration officers"** via [Houston Chronicle](https://substack.com/redirect/70d98824-e22c-4e33-89dc-d4cfd7b2e847?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) - A federal prosecutor says tests on "a white crystal-like substance" found inside the van of a man shot to death by immigration officers in Houston last month showed the material was not methamphetamine.

U.S. Attorney **Aaron Reitz** confirmed the tests were negative for meth in a statement to The Texas Tribune, the news organization reported Thursday.

**Lorenzo Salgado Araujo** , 52, was killed July 7 when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in unmarked vehicles chased his white work van through the streets of Houston, then shot him through the window. He had been driving his work crew, including his brother, to a construction site. _([HOU CHRON](https://substack.com/redirect/70d98824-e22c-4e33-89dc-d4cfd7b2e847?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Why Houston's bid for an NHL expansion team is different under Dan Friedkin"** via [Houston Chronicle](https://substack.com/redirect/38b792f7-3d02-4e51-a69a-fcfe01a78c4a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Greg Rajan** - Houston billionaire Dan Friedkin, no stranger to pro sports with his European soccer teams, is pursuing an NHL expansion franchise in Texas. Houston and Austin are being considered, with a decision to come in December.

The man who could bring Houston the city's long-awaited NHL franchise is staying mum for the moment. But as billionaire **Dan Friedkin** decides between Houston and Austin for the location of the NHL's 33rd franchise, it's becoming clear this effort is much further along than previous endeavors in the city's decades-long quest for a team in hockey's top league.

A spokesman for Pursuit Sports, Dan Friedkin's company dedicated to the family's sports properties, politely declined comment when asked how things are progressing nearly two months since NHL commissioner **Gary Bettman** announced the exploration of expansion in Texas. But deputy commissioner **Bill Daly** , the longtime right-hand man for Bettman, said Friedkin has brought a different dynamic than previous suitors.

Daly told the Houston Chronicle, "I think there's always a variety of kind of environmental factors that can play into any particular situation, either positive or negative," Daly said. "In Houston's case in particular, (it's) whether there's a suitable venue in which the hockey team can play. And so one of the things that I think the Friedkin Group brings and probably could be the first group to bring to this equation is a willingness to find and establish a suitable facility for a hockey team. _([HOU CHRON](https://substack.com/redirect/38b792f7-3d02-4e51-a69a-fcfe01a78c4a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Houston area toddler at center of fight over brain death testing has died"** via [The Texas Tribune](https://substack.com/redirect/a820f168-1c1c-4a51-be6f-0e8e2d089b38?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Katlyn Ma** -**Annelise Camp** , a 2-year-old girl whose parents sued to stop Texas Children's Hospital from testing if she's brain dead, died Monday after her breathing tube was removed.

In social media posts, Annelise's family confirmed her death, ending a months-long legal dispute over whether hospitals need a family's consent to test a patient for brain death. The New York Times first reported her death.

"Annelise is now with Jesus," wrote her parents, **Johnston Camp** and **Joy Camp** , on the family's GoFundMe page. "We pray that her legacy continues to inspire compassion, encourage meaningful change, and bring hope to families for years to come."

Rep. **Steve Toth** , R-The Woodlands, who has been in contact with Annelise's father, said the family just told Annelise's two siblings of her death. "It's been traumatic for the family," said Steve Toth in an interview with the Texas Tribune. _([TX TRIB](https://substack.com/redirect/a820f168-1c1c-4a51-be6f-0e8e2d089b38?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Two soldiers dead in Fort Hood military chopper crash"** via [KXAN](https://substack.com/redirect/7b04053b-3b24-48d3-8f42-8935a3f10d5a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) - Authorities are responding to a Fort Hood military chopper crash in Bell County. This was a 1st Cavalry Division 'Apache'; helicopter with two soldiers on board. Both have been pronounced dead.

The deceased service members will be transported to Carl R. Darnall Army Medical Center, according to the Fort Hood Media Center. The crash happened around 1:30 p.m. in a private field, according to the Bell County Sheriff's Office.

"Our immediate priority is securing the site and supporting the initial response efforts," said Brig. Gen. **Ethan Diven** , acting commanding general. Our thoughts are with the crew and their families as we await further information.

The crash has caused a rapid grass fire, leading to closures on FM-2843. Air units were seen responding to the fire sparked by the crash, which sent smoke billowing into the sky. Multiple fire units are responding. _([KXAN](https://substack.com/redirect/7b04053b-3b24-48d3-8f42-8935a3f10d5a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Trial lawyers, once a force for Democrats, reclaim political clout in Texas GOP's MAGA wing"** via [The Texas Tribune](https://substack.com/redirect/62432f54-9a45-4257-95ff-a4e2097563b3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Eleanor Klibanoff** - When **Armin Mizani** won the GOP primary for a north Texas House district in March, warning bells went off in certain Republican circles. It's not his political ideology. Mizani is a die-hard conservative who, as mayor of Keller, proudly partnered with federal immigration officials, denounced Sharia law and slashed property taxes.

It's his profession: Mizani is a personal injury lawyer, a career path once so closely intertwined with Democratic politics that both were pushed to the sidelines when Republicans gained control in Texas in the early 2000s. But now, a quarter century later, some trial lawyers are reclaiming their political relevance by aligning with Republicans.

The Texas Trial Lawyers Association, once the de facto war chest of the Texas Democratic Party, sponsored the state GOP convention. Wealthy personal injury lawyers are throwing cash behind conservative candidates, including Attorney General **Ken Paxton** 's Senate bid. And trial lawyers themselves are running as Republicans on their record representing "average Texans against powerful insurance companies," as Mizani said at a candidate forum.

"America First Republicans care more about how policy impacts everyday Texans than about corporate profits and special interests," Mizani added. Hidden from view of the average Texas voter, this realignment is the result of a complete upheaval of the power base within the Texas GOP. The traditional, business-first Republicans who rose to power by sharply restricting personal injury suits have been supplanted by a MAGA wing that scorns "corporate welfare," crusades against Big Tech, and is open to the idea that Texas' legal system has gotten too friendly to big business over the little guy. _([TX TRIB](https://substack.com/redirect/62432f54-9a45-4257-95ff-a4e2097563b3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

* * *
**2026**
**" Are Greg Abbott's new data center restrictions enough to sway rural voters?"** via [Houston Chronicle](https://substack.com/redirect/baeb08b2-816b-4d0d-9bc7-aee7c903ce8a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Benjamin Wermund** - Texas Governor **Greg Abbott** has spent much of the summer working to quell a roiling backlash to data centers in rural parts of the state where Republicans need to maintain strong support in the upcoming midterms.

He's called on lawmakers to strip their lucrative tax breaks next session, and ordered regulators to set new restrictions and conduct an audit before permitting any more projects to break ground.

But those efforts aren't winning over all skeptics. Several rural Republicans say they don't trust the governor whose biggest donors are increasingly invested in the data center boom and who praised Texas as the "epicenter of AI development" as recently as November.

"Rural Texas is not buying Abbott's thing," said **Mason McAllister** , a resident of a small town in Grayson County in North Texas. "The guys around here are fired up. **" Are There Really Democrats for Paxton and Republicans for Talarico?"** via [Texas Monthly](https://substack.com/redirect/7d619a70-e61c-4390-b105-e1194b9063cf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Christopher Hooks** - Casting ballots across party lines used to be pretty common in Texas: It was a behavior folks had to unlearn. In 1952, Texas Republicans knew any gubernatorial candidate they put forward would lose to the conservative Democratic candidate and decided to give him their nomination too, so that the final result on Election Day was **Allan Shivers** versus Allan Shivers, 73 to 25. This produced a couple of decades in which Texas politics was unpredictable--in a way it wasn't before and hasn't been since. **" Old EDS 'God Pod' to be imploded for AT&T's new billion-dollar HQ"** via [Dallas Morning News](https://substack.com/redirect/f1f74b85-eff4-4231-bf7e-468e13ba3477?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)' **Nick Wooten** - Sunday marks the end of an era and the start of something new in Plano. Additional portions of the old Electronic Data Systems campus, including the futuristic executive office building dubbed the "God Pod," will be imploded Sunday morning. The demolition is no surprise. Telecommunications giant AT&T planned to demolish the entire slate of buildings and parking garages to build its new billion-dollar-plus global headquarters at 5400 Legacy Drive.

Plano officials told The Dallas Morning News "a planned controlled demolition" will take place on Parkwood Boulevard between Legacy Drive and Democracy Drive around 8 a.m. AT&T declined to comment on the demolition. KDC, the developer of AT&T's campus, said construction is underway and demolition has begun at the site's north end. The company declined to provide any additional details.

EDS' move to Plano in the late 1980s was the first in a flurry of moves that helped establish the Collin County suburb as a headquarters hotspot. EDS founder **Ross Perot** purchased 2,700 acres in west Plano to establish the master-planned Legacy business park. For his son, real estate developer **Ross Perot Jr.** , the site holds special memories. He learned to fly a helicopter there, and he remembers riding horses when the Plano parcels his father owned were just raw land. Perot Jr. said he toured the old EDS site a few months back with AT&T CEO **John Stankey** just before demolition began. Perot Jr. said he won't attend Sunday's implosion. _([DMN](https://substack.com/redirect/f1f74b85-eff4-4231-bf7e-468e13ba3477?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Pharmaceutical giant to bring $2.3B manufacturing plant, 500 jobs to Houston"** via [Houston Chronicle](https://substack.com/redirect/ac989226-9ad6-423d-aa0d-6b23f26d7f2c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Erica Grieder** - Bristol Myers Squibb announced Monday that it will build a $2.3 billion advanced manufacturing facility in Houston's Generation Park, a coup for the region's growing biotech sector.

The new facility in northeast Houston will cover 600,000 square feet and create 500 jobs, according to the New Jersey-based pharmaceutical giant. Construction will begin next year and is expected to be completed by 2030, the company said, creating about 2,000 jobs during that three-year period.

The new facility "is designed to grow in scale, capability and workforce for decades to come," **Bristol Myers Squibb** said in a statement. "BMS envisions this site growing in scale and capability well beyond its opening configuration." _([HOU CHRON](https://substack.com/redirect/ac989226-9ad6-423d-aa0d-6b23f26d7f2c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**TEXANS IN DC**
**" Cornyn Urges DHS to Hear Texas Concerns Before Big Bend Border Barrier Construction"** via [Texas Border Business](https://substack.com/redirect/67396605-3c49-4e75-9177-012cbd9e5dc2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) - Senator **John Cornyn** , R-Texas, has asked the Department of Homeland Security to meet with Texas stakeholders before proceeding with additional construction of physical border barriers in Big Bend National Park and Big Bend Ranch State Park.

Cornyn said Texas supports federal efforts to secure the U.S.-Mexico border while asking DHS to consider concerns specific to the Big Bend area.

"Texas has always worked cooperatively with the Department of Homeland Security ('DHS' or 'Department') on border security, and we fully support strong border security measures to stop the flow of illegal aliens, drugs, and potential terrorists into the United States," Cornyn wrote.

According to Cornyn, stakeholders contend that the geography surrounding Big Bend already presents significant obstacles to unauthorized crossings, and he described concerns from people who live and work near the parks about the potential environmental, cultural and economic effects of constructing a physical wall and related infrastructure, in a letter to DHS Secretary **Markwayne Mullin**. _([Texas Border Business](https://substack.com/redirect/67396605-3c49-4e75-9177-012cbd9e5dc2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Ted Cruz's college sports bill left in limbo as U.S. Senate takes August recess"** via Texas Tribune's **Samanta Habashy** - Sen. **Ted Cruz 's** bill that would place sweeping new regulations on college sports failed to reach the floor this week before the Senate gaveled out for recess, imperiling its chances to become law this year as the midterm elections approach.

The measure, coined the Protect College Sports Act, had gained a sudden burst of momentum with support from the Southeastern Conference and Big Ten, after spending weeks in limbo. It advanced out of the Senate Commerce Committee, which Cruz chairs, before the chamber was scheduled to adjourn Friday. President **Donald Trump** urged senators to stay until they got through a pile-up of his legislative priorities, including the college sports bill.

But the bill never came up on the floor before the chamber gaveled out at 3:56 a.m. Senators could still pass the bill after their scheduled return to Capitol Hill after Labor Day. Last week, Cruz and other lawmakers, along with White House officials, negotiated a package of concessions with Big Ten and SEC leaders, who until then had refused to back the bill.

"Without this Bill, millions of young Athletes will be hurt, programs will be canceled, Women's and Olympic Sports will go away, the fans will be robbed, and Universities will go broke," **Donald Trump** posted on social media Friday afternoon, urging the Senate to stop "grandstanding" and pass it before leaving town. Cruz's bill would place a host of new regulations on the free-for-all system that has emerged since the NCAA in 2021 allowed college athletes to profit off their name, image and likeness, followed by a settlement a few years later that required the NCAA and athletic conferences to share revenue with athletes. _([ABC13 Houston](https://substack.com/redirect/355b6b60-a3fb-4cd3-b2b0-0c9d570edd30?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_
